title: The Protestants in turn grant it was not natural as constituting nature; many allow supernatural gifts and needed grace
source_text: XLVI. Vicissim vero Protestantes Doctoribus Scholae Romanae concedunt justitiam Originalem non fuisse primo homini naturalem, quatenus naturale significat, id quod naturam constituit, aut quod necessario, sive modo physico, fluit ex humanae naturae principiis. Ac praeterea multi Scholae Reformatae Doctores non negant primum hominem habuisse dona quaedam supernaturalia: & gratiam quandam homini, etiam innocenti, necessariam fuisse, ut recte & secundum justitiam operaretur. Quin eorum nonnulli justitiam Originalem ex naturae viribus non fluxisse fatentur.
pass_a_gloss: But in turn the Protestants grant to the Doctors of the Roman School that Original justice was not natural to the first man, insofar as natural signifies that which constitutes nature, or what necessarily, or in a physical way, flows from the principles of human nature. And moreover many Doctors of the Reformed School do not deny that the first man had certain supernatural gifts: and that a certain grace was necessary to man, even innocent, so that he might work rightly and according to justice. Nay some of them confess that Original justice did not flow from the powers of nature.
pass_b_english: The Protestants, for their part, grant the teachers of the Roman school that original righteousness was not natural to the first man in the sense of what makes up nature, or of what flows necessarily, that is physically, from the principles of human nature.

Many teachers of the Reformed school also do not deny that the first man had some supernatural gifts, and that even innocent man needed some grace in order to act rightly and righteously. Some of them even admit that original righteousness did not flow from the powers of nature.

choices.why: Fateri is a concession; 'admit' keeps the concessive tone.
